title: PASS 22/22
notes:
• Open cold. Don't introduce yourself yet. Read the green line, pause, then the last line.
  • Movie trick: show the ending first, then rewind. The audience spends the talk wondering how we got there.

title: Set Goal. Start Loop. Sleep.
notes:
• Hi Salem, I'm Somasundaram Mahesh, Somu for short. Founding AI engineer, and I co-founded United by AI. Show of hands: who has used an AI agent to write code? Keep it up if it ever told you "done" and it wasn't.
  • Keep your eye on those hands. That's the whole talk.
  • Now rewind: "This story starts at work, on a normal afternoon."

title: At work, I asked Claude Code to build something.
notes:
• Nothing exotic. It had a few phases, each one building on the last.
  • Keep this vague on purpose. What it was doesn't matter. What happened does.

title: A few minutes later
notes: • Pause on this. Let the room enjoy the green tick. Everyone has seen this message.

title: It wasn't.
notes:
• The bars are illustrative, not a log. Say "it would finish part of it and call the whole thing done".
  • The key word is "every time". This isn't a bug, it's a pattern.

title: So what did I do?
notes:
• Adjust the exact words to what you actually typed. The point: I kept nudging, checking, nudging.
  • "You're right" gets a laugh every time.

title: The agent wasn't the bottleneck. I was.
notes:
• This is the thesis. Slow down here.
  • Three jobs I was doing by hand: keep it going (loop), decide if it's done (checker), wake it up (alarm). Tonight we hand all three to the machine.

title: 22:45 · The problem.
notes: • My story is failure number one. There are three more, and you've probably met them too.

title: Four ways an agent fails when you look away.
notes:
• Stops early: says "done" when it isn't. That's my story.
  • Cheats: makes the check pass instead of the code.
  • Waits: asks a question at 11pm, you see it at 8am.
  • Breaks things: one bad command on your real machine.
  • Ask the room which one they've hit. Most will say one and two. Watch the tracker in the top right: these four stay red until we fix them.

title: It stops early.
notes:
• By default, the model decides when it's done. Nobody wrote down what "done" means, so it makes it up.
  • Models are optimistic. "Probably done" feels like done.
  • Long, multi-phase work makes it worse: the plan slides out of view.
  • Classic exchange: "All tests pass ✅" / "which tests did you run?" / "I didn't run them, but the changes look correct."

title: It cheats.
notes:
• Not on purpose. A failing test is often easier to change than the code. The agent is rewarded for green, so the test becomes the target.
  • Also seen: skipping the test, mocking the thing under test, catching and swallowing the error.
  • Lesson: whoever writes the code must not be the one grading it.

title: It waits for you.
notes:
• Eight hours of compute, zero minutes of work. The agent was polite. You were asleep.
  • Permission prompts are good when you're watching. They're a wall when you're not. Fix later: answer the questions before you leave.

title: It breaks things.
notes:
• The wrong folder: a cleanup command, one directory too high. The wrong branch: a force push to main at 3am. The wrong hands: a web page with hidden instructions, and your keys sitting right there.
  • To run unattended, you turn permission prompts off. Then the machine is the only seatbelt.

title: It already happened.
notes:
• Real incident, July 2025: a Replit agent deleted SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin's production database during a declared code freeze, then said it "panicked".
  • The fix wasn't a better prompt. It was dev/prod separation, one-click restore and a planning-only mode. Keep this in mind for harness part 6.

title: Every failure has a fix.
notes:
• This is the map for the rest of the talk.
  • And the thing that holds all of it together has a name: the harness.

title: 22:58 · Set Goal.
notes: • Fixes failures one and two. The single most useful skill in this talk.

title: A prompt is a request. A goal is a finish line.
notes:
• Left is what I typed. The agent decides when it's done. It decided early.
  • Right is what I should have typed. Anyone can check it, including another machine.
  • If you can't tell whether it's done, neither can the agent.

title: A good goal is a yes / no question.
notes: • pstack calls it a "checkable predicate". Every example here, a script can answer.

title: Fix these goals.
notes:
• 30 seconds per card. Take two answers, then reveal.
  • This is the one skill they can use tomorrow with zero paid tools.

title: Every agent now has /goal.
notes:
• Claude Code: /goal keeps taking turns until the condition holds. A separate model checks it after every turn. Headless: claude -p "/goal ...".
  • Codex: /goal with pause, resume, clear, and a budget. "The evidence decides."
  • Two companies, same command. If I'd had this for my multi-phase build, "continue" would have typed itself. Watch the tracker: 01 just turned green.

title: The author is never the critic.
notes:
• In Claude Code's /goal, a fresh model checks the condition after each turn.
  • pstack goes further: the judge comes from a different model family. Scripts are best of all. They don't get optimistic.

title: Lock the finish line.
notes:
• The tests and the checker are hashed in a LOCK file. If the agent edits the test to win, check.mjs fails with: "The finish line is not yours to move."
  • This is from the demo repo we'll see at the end. 02 turns green.

title: 23:04 · Start Loop.
notes: • Fixes failure three. Remember: I was the loop. Now we replace me.

title: My "continue", automated
notes:
• Geoffrey Huntley calls it the Ralph loop. Each pass is a fresh agent. The plan lives in a file: read it, do one thing, commit, exit, repeat.
  • A YC hackathon team ran it overnight and woke up to 6 shipped repos.
  • One line of bash is the thing I was doing by hand all afternoon.

title: Three ways to wake the agent up.
notes:
• /goal: one task, keep going until done. /loop: nothing to wait on, just re-check. Events: you're waiting on something real.
  • Rule of thumb: if there's an event, watch the event and keep a slow timer as backup. Don't poll CI every minute, get woken when it finishes.

title: One iteration.
notes: • Step 4: the agent throws away work that didn't help. When did you last delete code that didn't help?

title: Answer its questions before you leave.
notes:
• Four lines, four jobs. The permission line kills the 11:42pm question. The escape hatch beats eight hours of creative goal reinterpretation.
  • This exact file is GOAL.md in the demo repo.

title: 23:05 · The harness.
notes: • Zoom out. The goal, the check, the loop, the contract: none of that is the model.

title: Agent = Model + Harness
notes:
• The model reads the context and picks the next action. That's all it does.
  • The harness is all the code that turns that choice into work. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Antigravity are all harnesses.
  • My "done" problem was never a model problem. It was a harness problem. Next: eight parts, one slide each.

title: The loop
notes:
• The loop sends the context to the model, runs whatever tools it asks for, feeds the results back in, and decides when the task is finished.
  • Example: Claude Code reads a file, runs the tests, sees 3 failures, edits, runs again. Each round trip is one turn. /goal adds the rule for when to stop.
  • The "done?" gate is the part that failed me: the loop let the model decide.

title: Tools and sandbox
notes:
• Tools give the model a terminal, files, a browser and your apps. The sandbox runs every task inside its own isolated computer, so a bad command stays inside.
  • Example: a Cursor cloud agent gets its own VM. A Claude Code cloud session gets a fresh container with only the repo it needs. Delete everything in there? Nothing you care about is gone.

title: Subagents
notes:
• Subagents take side tasks off the main agent and run them in parallel, each with a fresh context window, and send back only a short summary.
  • Example: pstack's /how sends 2 to 4 cheap explorers into different corners of the codebase, then one strong model writes a single explanation. The main agent never sees the 40 files they read.
  • For a multi-phase build: one subagent per phase, one more to review each phase.
  • Anthropic's multi-agent research (June 2025): subagents beat a single agent by about 90% on their research eval but used roughly 15x the tokens, and an early version spawned 50 subagents for simple questions. Add a second agent only when the first is drowning.

title: Context management
notes:
• Context management decides what the model sees on every turn, loads skills and files only when the task needs them, and summarizes old history before the window fills.
  • Example: the harness shows the model a one-line description of each skill and loads the full file only when it's needed. 50 skills cost almost nothing until one is used.
  • Long multi-phase runs are exactly where the plan drops out of view. Keep it in a file, not in the chat.
  • Anthropic calls the failure "context rot": recall drops as the context grows. Aim for the smallest set of high-signal tokens. Karpathy calls the craft context engineering.

title: Memory
notes:
• Memory stores progress notes, git history and skills on disk, so a new session reads what the last one did and picks up where it stopped.
  • The checklist is ticked by the check passing, not by the agent saying so.
  • Lauren Tan: "your codebase is the ultimate form of memory."
  • Three techniques Anthropic describes: note-taking (a NOTES.md the agent reads back), compaction (summarize and restart), and just-in-time retrieval (keep links, load when needed).

title: Guardrails
notes:
• Guardrails hold risky actions like emails, payments and deletes for your approval, keep real credentials outside the sandbox, and give a prompt injection no credentials to steal.
  • Example: work on a branch, never main. Allow git and npm test, nothing else. The GitHub token lives in a proxy outside the box, so the agent can push a PR but can't read the key.
  • Guardrails are what make "don't ask me" safe to say. Remember the deleted database: a prompt saying "don't touch prod" is a wish. No prod credentials in the box is a guardrail.

title: The lethal trifecta.
notes:
• Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" (June 2025): private data, plus untrusted content (a web page, an email, an issue), plus any way to talk to the outside world, equals a data theft risk.
  • A prompt injection hidden in the untrusted content can tell the agent to send your private data out. Break any one of the three, or put a human gate on the send.
  • Students: check every agent you build against this. It takes ten seconds.

title: Verification
notes:
• Verification stops a summary that only sounds finished. It runs tests, browser checks or a separate grader, and only then lets the agent say done.
  • Not "I fixed it". Show me the failing test, then the passing test. Show me the before and after screenshot.
  • Lauren Tan: "The bottleneck with agents is verification." pstack ranks a verification skill as the single best investment. If you only build one part of the harness, build this one.

title: Observability
notes:
• Observability traces every model call and tool call, spots the agent repeating the same failed edit, and pushes it to try a different approach.
  • Without traces, you find out at 8am that it tried the same fix 200 times.

title: 8 parts, 4 failures, fixed.
notes: • One look back. Ask: which part would have saved my afternoon? Answer: verification, then the loop.

title: pstack
notes:
• Lauren Tan (poteto): React Compiler core team, ex Meta and Netflix. Built pstack at Cursor, now at SpaceXAI. Open sourced in May 2026 after Cursor's team used it 10,000 times in one week.
  • Her line on agents: "new hires in a constant state of amnesia and idiocy. Capable yet stupid, and very teachable." pstack is the teaching.

title: One router. Many playbooks.
notes: • You type one command. The router reads your task and picks the right recipe. Nothing loads by surprise: 53 of 54 skills only run when called.

title: Name the goal and the proof. Never the method.
notes:
• Compare with my "Build it. All the phases." Same length, completely different outcome.
  • Her advice: don't list skills, don't lead with your theory of the bug.

title: A skill is written experience.
notes:
• A skill is a folder with one SKILL.md file. Plain Markdown. The description says when to use it, the body says how.
  • The agent sees only the one-line description until it needs the rest. Same format in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex.
  • This is a real pstack skill, about 34 words. If you can write a README, you can write a skill.

title: Your agent forgets everything. Every single morning.
notes:
• Watch the memory bars: the sun comes up and they empty. A skill arrives and they refill.
  • Lauren Tan: "Agents are like new hires in a constant state of amnesia and idiocy. They're capable yet stupid, and very teachable."
  • A chat correction dies with the chat. A skill lives in the repo: every run, every parallel agent, every teammate's agent gets it.

title: Every scar becomes a skill.
notes:
• Lauren Tan: "I never set out to build pstack. I just started turning every recurring failure mode into a skill. The agents improved because their instructions carried the scars from previous runs."
  • Step 5 surprises people: pstack's history has passes that cut 600 to 700 lines at a time because newer models stopped needing them.
  • Her rule for when to add one: when the same failure shows up twice.

title: The skill I should have had.
notes:
• This is the "done" problem from the start of the talk, as a skill. Four lines.
  • And the last sentence is the correction ladder: a skill is good, a check is better.

title: Don't fix it twice.
notes:
• Every time you correct your agent, ask how to make that correction unnecessary. Climb as high as you can.
  • From Lauren's post in August. Rung 4 she marks "ngmi": not gonna make it.
  • Our LOCK file is rung 2: a check, not a request.

title: Three loop rules worth stealing.
notes:
• If a change didn't move the check, it doesn't ride along. Stuck? Change approach: don't quit, don't spin. Moving the finish line to declare victory is losing.
  • Plus a decision log every iteration, so you audit decisions in the morning, not transcripts. Rule three is why we have the LOCK file.

title: What it costs.
notes:
• Tokens: reviewer panels and verifier swarms add up. Slower, pricier, more correct. Ceremony: heavy for a two-line fix, most changes need none of it.
  • Prose only guides: only scripts enforce, so rules keep moving into code. One person's style: her models, her habits, build your own on top.
  • Her own words: "a low trust loop is just a waste of tokens." Productivity numbers online are self-reported. Take the ideas, not the numbers.

title: 23:06 · Sleep.
notes: • Fixes failure four, and lets you actually close the lid.

title: Your laptop is a bad place for a loop.
notes:
• It sleeps: lid closes, Wi-Fi drops, battery dies at 2am. It's crowded: two agents fight each other (and you) for the same files. It's yours: your keys, your cookies, your bank tab.
  • So move the loop to a machine that isn't yours, with only the keys the task needs. Harness parts 2 and 6, made physical. 04 turns green: all four fixed.

title: Cloud agents + Automations
notes:
• Every agent gets its own VM: terminal, browser, desktop. Start from the editor, your phone, Slack or GitHub. It attaches videos and screenshots to the PR as proof.
  • Automations start them on a schedule or an event: a merged PR, a Slack message, an alert. Nobody types a prompt; the event is the prompt.
  • 30%+ of PRs merged at Cursor are made by agents running on their own in cloud sandboxes (Cursor, Feb 2026).

title: Cloud sessions + scheduled tasks
notes:
• Cloud sessions: start from claude.ai/code, the phone app, or claude --cloud. Close the laptop, it keeps going and opens a PR, then watches its own PR: fixes CI, answers review comments.
  • Scheduled tasks: a saved prompt + repos + connectors that fires on a schedule, an API call, or a GitHub event. "Every night at 2am: pull the top bug, attempt a fix, open a PR."
  • The demo repo for this talk was built and dry-run in one of these cloud sessions.

title: Buzz: agents as teammates
notes:
• Buzz: Slack-like, but every agent has its own identity. Bring any agent: Claude Code, Codex, goose. Open source, self-host it.
  • How Block builds Buzz, in Buzz: a human opens a channel and states the goal, agents research, build and test in the thread, a different agent reviews the builder, humans decide what merges.
  • Same shape as this whole talk: goal, loop, separate critic, human signs off. Just with a team of agents. The chat is illustrative.

title: Where should your loop live?
notes: • Start with /goal on your laptop. Move to the cloud when you want to close the lid.

title: 07:30 · Morning.
notes: • Now the payoff. I built a small repo to run this exactly the way the talk describes.

title: The receipt.
notes:
• Real run with claude -p "/goal node check.mjs prints PASS". About two minutes, because the task is small. The point is I wasn't there.
  • "Done" here isn't a sentence from the agent. It's PASS from a script it couldn't touch.

title: Read 10 rows, not 8 hours.
notes:
• parseDuration is my favourite row: it found an edge case on its own and wrote down why.
  • pstack does this with /show-me-your-work, and a reviewer from a different model reads the log first.

title: Before and after.
notes: • Close the loop on the story. Same agent, same model. The only difference is the harness around it.

title: Earn the sleep first.
notes:
• Checklist from pstack's guide: you've done the task once by hand or watched an agent do it; the agent has the tools you'd use (tests, logs, screenshots); every step proves its work and can stop the line; you've read a few runs and turned repeat failures into checks.
  • Until all four hold, run the loop while you watch. The quote is Geoffrey Huntley's, about running loops without a sandbox.
  • Risk tiers: low-risk actions run alone, medium ones run and leave a trail, high ones (send, pay, delete, publish) wait for a yes. Move an action down a tier only after many approvals with no edits.

title: AI doesn't add judgment. It multiplies it.
notes:
• Read the bottom row first: without AI, weak judgment is dead weight, good judgment is steady hands.
  • Now add AI to both. Weak judgment becomes a slop cannon: more output, same bad calls, faster. Good judgment becomes a turbo brain.
  • Tie back: my afternoon was AI without the judgment written down. Everything tonight, the yes/no goal, the locked check, the harness, is how you put your judgment into the loop so it multiplies the right thing.
  • Framework from danhock.com (shared by Justin Elze, TrustedSec).

title: Your job changed.
notes: • The skill that matters isn't prompting anymore. It's knowing what done looks like.

title: Try it before you sleep.
notes: • Pick one small thing in your project, write a goal that's a yes/no question, run /goal in Claude Code or Codex or install pstack, go to sleep. Scan the QR: github.com/msomu/overnight-loop. Clone it, run ./ralph.sh or /goal, then ./morning.sh. Tag me on X (@msomuin) or LinkedIn with what you woke up to.
